author: blu
body: Both wrap, which is what a list a person arrows through should do. An empty result is the case that has to be said out loud: wrapping upward lands on `visible - 1`, which is -1 when the filter matched nothing, and a highlight of -1 indexes one before the start of the list it belongs to. There is nothing to highlight in an empty list, so the answer is zero.

author: blu
body: The match ignores case, on both sides. A palette is a thing a person types into in a hurry and the labels are written for reading, so a command called "Open folder" has to be findable by typing `open`. Matching the raw texts meant it was not: the query was compared against the label exactly, so a lowercase query missed every capitalised label and a capitalised query missed every lowercase one.

author: blu
body: Both sides are folded rather than just the query, because the labels come from the app and half of them are capitalised.

author: blu
body: Both ends are checked, not just the upper one. A highlight below zero passed the single `<` test and indexed one before the start of the list, which is the word holding the list's own capacity.

author: blu
body: What that cost is different in the two functions and worth separating. `palette-selected-command` answered **`Just` a command whose every field was empty**, which a caller cannot tell from a real one and would dispatch; removing its lower bound moves the reading from `none` to `[]`, so that guard is fired by `codex/test/palette-filter`. `palette-confirm` also read out of range, but the action it got back happened to be zero, which is exactly what it answers when it refuses. Removing ITS lower bound moves no line of the test, and that is recorded here rather than left for someone to find and delete: the guard is there to stop the read, not to change an answer, and no assertion in this tree distinguishes the two.

author: blu
body: The window is the smallest one ending at the highlight, so it does not move until the selection would leave it and the first screenful is the first twelve.

author: blu
body: A key is what `UI chapter KeyInput` says it is: a character is its CCE code point and a named key is a constant at or above `key-named-base`. This handler took a raw PS/2 Set-1 SCANCODE, which is a third thing again -- neither the CCE identity `poll-key` hands out nor the virtual key codes the other widgets in this quire had. It tested 1, 36 and 37, which as scancodes are Escape and the j and k keys; as CCE they are the newline, `x` and `q`. Fed what the quire actually produces, every arm missed and the palette could not be closed or walked.
